- **𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀: 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 𝗠𝗲𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗔𝗜 For decades, the leadership model was relatively simple: Business leaders set the strategy. Technology leaders delivered it. AI is changing that. Today, strategy, technology, data, and operating models are becoming increasingly interconnected. Decisions about growth, productivity, customer experience, and innovation are now deeply influenced by AI, data, and digital capabilities. This is why I believe the biggest AI capability gap may not be in our technology teams. It may be in leadership. We are entering the era of the bilingual leader. Not leaders who are engineers, but leaders who can speak the language of business, value, customers, and strategy while understanding enough about data, platforms, architecture, AI, and agents to make better decisions. Because increasingly: - Your AI strategy is constrained by your data. - Your speed is constrained by your architecture. - Your ability to scale is constrained by your technology foundations. - Your ability to create value is constrained by how effectively you redesign the business processes around these capabilities. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is building the organizational capability to turn AI into sustainable business value. It requires building AI muscle: the ability to repeatedly apply, learn, scale, govern, and transform. Business leaders need greater technology and AI fluency. The leaders who can move seamlessly across: 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 → 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 → 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 → 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 → 𝗔𝗜 → 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 → 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲 will be best positioned to transform AI from experimentation into enterprise advantage. Perhaps this is the new leadership equation: 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗹𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲 + 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗵 + 𝗔𝗜 𝗠𝘂𝘀𝗰𝗹𝗲 = 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 The AI era won't be defined solely by better technology. - **What does intelligence cost your enterprise? McKinsey’s recent work on the economics of AI raises an important question for leaders: as AI moves from individual agents to workflows and increasingly complex enterprise operating systems, how should we think about cost vs value? For years, we have measured technology through infrastructure costs, licenses, cloud consumption and recently tokens and model costs. But none of these measures what the enterprise actually needs from AI: Better decisions, Faster actions or Better outcomes. Perhaps the unit of AI economics should eventually move from cost per token to cost per intelligent decision. Think about the full stack Agentic Workflow: Data → Context → Intelligence → Decision → Action → Outcome Every layer has a cost. But every layer also has the potential to create value. The real opportunity is therefore not simply making AI cheaper. But increasing the economic yield of enterprise intelligence: - How quickly can we turn data into insight? - How reliably can we turn insight into decisions? - How efficiently can we turn decisions into action? - And how much measurable value does that action create? The question is no longer just: “What is the ROI of this AI use case?” It becomes: “How effectively does our enterprise convert data and intelligence into better decisions, faster actions and better outcomes?” That, to me, is the next frontier: the economics of enterprise intelligence. #AI #EnterpriseAI #AILeadership #Data #DigitalTransformation #AgenticAI #CAIO**

- **After 15 years, I'm writing the hardest and most grateful LinkedIn post of my career: I'm leaving Novartis. Fifteen years ago I joined a company built on a simple idea: that innovation should reach the patients who need it, faster. I didn't know then how deeply that idea would shape me. In Poland, I learned the lesson that has stayed with me ever since: a breakthrough medicine means nothing until a patient can actually access it. That truth shaped how I've led ever since. In China, I helped build one of the most ambitious transformations in our industry: bringing innovative medicines to patients faster, in a market rewriting its own rules in real time. And for the last two years in Basel, as Chief Commercial Officer International, I found myself doing something I loved: closing the gap between a strategy on a slide and a launch in a patient's hands. I watched us get faster and more disciplined at the moment that matters the most: the launch itself; turning what used to be inconsistent into something we could deliver, every time and everywhere. Along the way, I've worked on medicines that changed how we treat cardiovascular disease, psoriasis, cancers, and multiple sclerosis. These aren't just products; they help patients who got more time and more life. Being part of that is a real honor and a privilege. None of it was mine alone. To Vas Narasimhan , Rob Kowalski , Patrick Horber, M.D. and Rahul S. , who gave me the trust and the platform to lead — thank you. To leaders who believed in me and built something extraordinary with me in China — thank you. To the CLS team and the China LT, who trusted a leader again and again, and to every colleague across geography and culture who became a friend along the way: you know who you are, and thank you. I'm proud of what we built together, and prouder still of how we built it: a team that debated hard, trusted fully, and never stopped aiming high. It has been an honor. Novartis didn't just give me a career. It gave me a purpose. More soon.**
